analysis.one_liner: Limits the Religious Freedom Restoration Act so it cannot override civil rights, wage, child labor, and health care protections.
analysis.headline: The Do No Harm Act was introduced in the Senate with 39 supporters and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993 (RFRA) lets people sue to exempt themselves from laws they say burden their religious exercise, even when that shifts costs onto others. The Do No Harm Act would say RFRA cannot be used to override laws against discrimination, laws requiring employers to pay wages and benefits or provide leave, laws protecting workplace collective activity and children, or laws ensuring access to health care including contraception. It would also block RFRA claims between two private parties unless the government itself is being sued, and bar using RFRA to deny people goods or services the government has promised them.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who would otherwise be denied wages, benefits, or leave their employer claims a religious exemption from; women seeking contraception coverage; LGBTQ people relying on anti-discrimination protections; children protected by child labor laws; and anyone receiving government-funded services who could otherwise be refused by a religious contractor.

how_it_helps.text: Blocks RFRA from being used to exempt employers from laws requiring wages, benefits, or leave [S2] [S3]
Protects anti-discrimination laws, including the Civil Rights Act and ADA, from RFRA override [S2] [S3]
Keeps RFRA from blocking access to health care items and services, including contraception coverage [S2] [S3]
Prevents people from using RFRA to deny others goods, services, or benefits the government has provided or agreed to provide [S2] [S3]
Limits RFRA lawsuits to cases where the government is a party, stopping one private party from suing another over a religious objection [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Employers who currently win religious exemptions from wage, benefit, or health coverage mandates; religious organizations and contractors that refuse services on religious grounds; and some religious individuals whose RFRA claims in civil-rights or health-care disputes would no longer be recognized.

drawbacks.text: Religious liberty advocates argue the bill guts RFRA's core protection and could force religious objectors, including religious hospitals and schools, to act against their beliefs [S3]
The health care provision is broad: it removes RFRA protection for any claim about 'access to' any health care item or service, which could reach disputes well beyond contraception coverage [S3]
The bill doesn't amend other federal religious exemption statutes, so cases governed by those laws rather than RFRA would be unaffected [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers and patients whose legal protections have been eroded by expanding RFRA claims, this bill restores clear legal ground. The cost falls on religious objectors who currently prevail in exemption claims, and critics reasonably warn that the health care language is sweeping. It doesn't ban any religious practice; it stops RFRA specifically from trumping a defined set of protections.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate in April 2023 and referred to the Judiciary Committee, which never scheduled a hearing or vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Booker introduced S.1206 with 38 Senate cosponsors on April 19, 2023 [S4] [S5]
The Senate referred it to the Judiciary Committee, where no action followed for the rest of the 118th Congress [S5]
No House companion or hearing is shown in the action history [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers seeking religious exemptions from wage, benefit, and health coverage laws retain the current legal status quo, since the bill never advanced.

for.name: Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action: no hearing, no markup, no vote, no floor referral before Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: All 39 supporters are Democrats or the Senate's Independent; no Republican cosponsor is listed [S4].

industries.industry: Religiously affiliated employers, hospitals, schools, and contractors
industries.note: These entities would lose RFRA as a legal tool to refuse coverage, wages, or services on religious grounds. Under the bill, they could no longer claim a religious exemption against anti-discrimination, wage, or health care mandates.
Employers who previously prevailed on RFRA claims to avoid wage, benefit, leave, or contraception coverage obligations would have to comply with those laws instead.
